title: Timeline fragmentation gap study: microburst vs steady-state
content:
Objective
- Short notes from a focused runbook-style investigation into latency fragmentation observed in production traces. Goal is to pin down why p95/p99 shows a multiplicative gap for microburst traffic vs steady-state steady QPS.

Context and why this matters
- Over the past 6 weeks we've seen increases in p95 for certain customer cohorts when they experience short 10-30 request bursts. Mean latency and p50 remain stable, but p95 and p99 jump 2-4x. This has direct SLA and UX impact for chat-style workloads.
- Hypothesis space: cold KV cache misses, batching alignment inefficiencies, CPU contention during token emission, network egress jitter, and retriable model fallbacks.

What I ran (quick checklist)
- Replayed 6k production traces sampled from last 7 days, grouped by burstiness metric and sequence length distribution.
- Collected trace spans: client-recv, ingress-queue, tokenization, request-routing, batching-wait, model-exec, kv-cache-lookup, postprocess, egress-write.
- For each trace computed per-stage duration and overlap with adjacent stages (concurrency window).

Cohorts used in this doc
- tiny: seqlen < 64, tokens emitted < 32, typical 1-3 parallel requests per burst
- medium: seqlen 64-256, tokens 32-128, parallel 3-10
- long: seqlen > 256, tokens > 128, parallel 1-4 (chat continuations)

Aggregate quantiles (end-to-end in ms)
- tiny: p50 38ms, p95 142ms, p99 293ms
- medium: p50 124ms, p95 446ms, p99 982ms
- long: p50 392ms, p95 1120ms, p99 2187ms

Observation 1 - fragmentation pattern
- Microburst traces (tiny cohort) show a bimodal p95: one mode near steady-state 60-80ms, second mode 180-400ms. The longer tail aligns with traces that incurred a batching-wait > 60ms plus a kv-cache miss.
- Steady-state traffic rarely shows batching-wait > 45ms.

Observation 2 - per-stage breakdowns for problematic tiny cohort traces (p95 bucket) average values in ms
- ingress-queue: 6
- tokenization: 4
- batching-wait: 86 (35% of total)
- model-exec: 38 (15%)
- kv-cache-lookup: 72 (30%)  // note: large variance, misses up to 240ms when falling back to cold path
- postprocess+egress: 20
- network egress jitter: 18
- total: 244ms (median of this p95 group)

Key micro-observation
- kv-cache lookups are sometimes routed to a slower read tier under contention, adding 40-200ms. This correlates with cache eviction spikes documented in RT-3410.
- Batching-wait increases when burst alignment leaves one request waiting for the next tick. The scheduler tick is currently 12ms aligned to a fixed window; bursts with staggered arrival times hit the tail.

Overlap analysis insight
- Many long-tail requests show positive overlap between batching-wait and model-exec on different requests, indicating head-of-line blocking across logical lanes. In practice a slow kv-cache miss for request A pushes request B into a later batch so B pays both wait and exec latency.

Short synthetic microbenchmark to reproduce
- 1000 bursts of 8 concurrent tiny requests with arrival jitter uniform 0-20ms to a 4-GPU pool with current batching config. Results: p95 increases from 90ms to 260ms when kv-cache warmup not enforced and when scheduler tick remains fixed.

Possible root causes ranked by likelihood
1) Cache routing fallback under contention. Evidence: traces with backend read-tier fallback show +60-200ms in kv lookup span. Correlates with cache eviction events. High likelihood.
2) Batching tick alignment policy. Fixed tick leads to quantized wait states; when bursts are misaligned many requests join next tick causing artificial extra wait. Medium-high likelihood.
3) Per-request lock contention in routing layer that amplifies when bursts create cross-lane head-of-line effects. Medium likelihood.
4) Network egress microbursts (socket slowdowns) adding jitter. Low-medium likelihood.

Quick mitigation experiments attempted
- Temporarily increased cache read parallelism for the affected customer pool: p95 improved 28% for tiny cohort during a 2 hour test window.
- Adjusted scheduler tick down from 12ms to 6ms on canary nodes: batching-wait p95 reduced from 86ms to 42ms but CPU cost increased ~6% and p50 unchanged.
- Warmup prefetch of KV keys on initial request for chat sessions reduced kv cache miss rate by 60% in sessionized traffic.

Proposed short-term actions (1-2 weeks)
- Deploy cache read routing fix from RT-3410 to 10% of capacity for affected regions. Monitor p95 and cache fallback rate. Owner: Luca.
- Canary reduced scheduler tick to 6ms on dedicated burst-friendly pools. Observe CPU and throughput. Owner: Sofia.
- Add a lightweight trace tag to mark cache fallback path for easier query. Owner: Priya.

Proposed medium-term actions (2-8 weeks)
- Replace fixed tick batching with adaptive micro-window that shortens when burstiness metric exceeds threshold. Coordinate with batching team and evaluate overhead. Owner: eng-serving-runtime.
- Add per-lane admission control to avoid HOl blocking where a lane with a slow external call prevents other lanes joining the same batch.
- Revisit kv-cache eviction policy to reduce cold fallback frequency for small, high-PPS keys.

Open questions and next probes
- What is the cost to reduce tick to 4ms on dedicated pools? Does p99 improve proportionally or only p95?
- Can we identify a small subset of keys responsible for most fallbacks and proactively pin them on hot tier?
- Is there a scheduler-level metric we can emit to quantify burst alignment efficiency per customer?

Appendix: useful queries and trace selectors used
- trace selector example: service:runtime and tag:batching and duration>100 and cohort=tiny
- kv fallback selector: span.name:kv-cache-lookup and span.attr.path:slow-read-tier
- burstiness metric: per-10s request count variance normalized by mean

Notes to self
- Keep this doc as working until we have replayed the next 48h of traces after the canary. Capture storage of sample traces in s3://rt-traces/burst-study/mar-2026.
- Sync with batching owners Mon morning 10am PST and file follow-up in RT-3499.

End of notes
